unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe professional appearance and grooming standards for the medical office.
- Explain the importance of reliability, attendance, and punctuality in patient care.
- Identify appropriate steps when running late or absent from work.
- Apply time-management and scheduling practices that support a dependable workplace.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a uniform as a team jersey. When players wear the right, tidy gear, the fans trust the team knows what it is doing.

### Question 2

Imagine working in a busy kitchen. You wear sturdy shoes so you don't slip or drop something on your toes. The medical office is the same idea.

### Question 3

A name badge is like a name tag at a big school event. It tells people who you are so they know who is helping them.

### Question 4

Imagine tying your hair back before baking so it doesn't fall into the food. Securing hair back keeps it neat and out of the way.

### Question 5

Germs like to hide under long nails and inside rings. Short, clean nails leave germs fewer places to hide.

### Question 6

Some people get sneezy or get a headache from strong perfume, like how some people sneeze near strong flowers. Offices keep scents light so everyone can breathe easily.

### Question 7

When you dress neatly, you look like you care about your job. That helps people feel they are in good hands.

### Question 8

If you spill something on your shirt at school, you change it when you can instead of wearing it all day. Same idea at work.

### Question 9

Think of a school uniform. It doesn't make you smarter, but it helps everyone look like they belong to the same team and are ready to learn.

### Question 10

When you don't know a rule, you ask the person in charge instead of guessing. That way you never break the rule by accident.

### Question 11

Different schools have different rules about what you can wear. You check your own school's rulebook rather than guessing.

### Question 12

When someone shows up neat and tidy, it says, 'I care about what I do.' That makes people trust them more.

### Question 13

When you work somewhere messy, like painting, you wear clothes that protect you and can be washed easily. Medical offices are similar.

### Question 14

Before school you check the mirror: hair brushed, shirt clean, name tag on. A quick check helps you start the day right.

### Question 15

When you feel nervous, seeing a person who looks neat and tells you their name makes you feel safer, like meeting a friendly helper.

### Question 16

Washing your hands and staying clean keeps germs away from other people, just like washing up before dinner.

### Question 17

You wash your hands many times a day, not just once, because germs keep getting on your hands all day long.

### Question 18

Staying clean and wearing fresh clothes is like keeping your school locker tidy so it doesn't smell bad.

### Question 19

When you have a cold, you cover your cough and wash your hands so your friends don't get sick too.

### Question 20

Some people start sneezing around strong perfume, like being near a very strong flower smell. Offices keep scents light to help everyone.

### Question 21

Brushing your teeth every day keeps your mouth healthy and your breath fresh, like cleaning your room keeps it nice.

### Question 22

Hand hygiene means cleaning your hands the right way, with soap and water or hand sanitizer.

### Question 23

Clean hands before touching things others will touch is a rule everyone follows, like washing hands before sharing snacks.

### Question 24

If something is bothering everyone, you tell the teacher quietly instead of shouting it in class. The teacher can fix it kindly.

### Question 25

Germs hide under long nails like crumbs hide under a table edge. Short, clean nails leave no place for them to hide.

### Question 26

A name tag only works if people can see it. It should face front so everyone knows who you are.

### Question 27

If you know a helper's name, you know who to thank or who to ask for again. A name badge makes that easy.

### Question 28

If you forget your name tag, you tell the teacher and get a temporary one instead of pretending you don't need it.

### Question 29

A badge is like a helper's name tag. It helps everyone know who belongs in the office and who is helping them.

### Question 30

A name tag tells you who someone is, but the rules about which doors they may open are kept in a separate list.

### Question 31

Your badge photo is like a school picture. You want to look neat so people can clearly see who you are.

### Question 32

Being reliable is like being the friend who always keeps their promises and shows up when they say they will.

### Question 33

If your job is to set the table, a reliable person sets all of it and speaks up if the plates are missing.

### Question 34

When everyone does their job on time, patients get seen quickly and safely, like a team passing the ball without dropping it.

### Question 35

If you can't finish your part of a group project, you tell your teammates early so they can help instead of waiting until it's too late.

### Question 36

A reliable person does the right thing all the time, not just when someone is watching.

### Question 37

Doing the boring chore you promised to do, like taking out the trash, shows you are trustworthy.

### Question 38

If you don't understand the directions, you ask the teacher before starting instead of guessing wrong.

### Question 39

Being dependable means people can trust you to do what you say you will do.

### Question 40

Imagine putting the wrong test paper in the wrong folder. The teacher might grade the wrong work. Filing correctly keeps everything safe.

### Question 41

If you can't finish because the glue is missing, you tell the teacher right away instead of sitting quietly.

### Question 42

A to-do list is like a shopping list. It helps you remember everything and do the important things first.

### Question 43

The friend who always does their chores without being asked is the one you call reliable.

### Question 44

Being on time means being in your seat ready to start when the bell rings, not walking in later.

### Question 45

If class starts at 8, you come a little early so your books are out and you're ready when the bell rings.

### Question 46

A team works only when every player shows up. If one is missing, the whole game is harder.

### Question 47

If you're running late, you call ahead and tell someone when you'll arrive so they aren't worried or caught off guard.

### Question 48

If the person who hands out lunches is absent, everyone waits longer. Missing one person slows the whole line.

### Question 49

Chronic absenteeism is missing work again and again without planning, not just one sick day.

### Question 50

If you leave early for school, a slow bus won't make you late. A little extra time is your safety net.

### Question 51

A start time is like the start of a race. You need to be at the line ready to go, not still getting ready.

### Question 52

Set your alarm with plenty of time, like a fire drill, so you can wake up, get ready, and arrive without rushing.

### Question 53

If you have the key and are late, you call the person in charge immediately so they can open up instead of leaving everyone locked out.

### Question 54

If you promised to help after school, you don't also plan something else at the same time. You keep your word.

### Question 55

Good attendance is like perfect school attendance: you're there every day unless you're truly sick and you tell someone.

### Question 56

Time management is like planning your homework so you finish the important parts first and don't rush at the last minute.

### Question 57

When you have lots of homework, you do what's due first and ask the teacher if you're not sure.

### Question 58

A planner is like a reminder note so you don't forget anything, not a way to put things off forever.

### Question 59

Leave extra time like you leave early for a trip, so a small delay doesn't make you miss everything else.

### Question 60

When you make a playdate, you check both calendars and write it down so no one is double-booked.

### Question 61

If two things need doing at once, you tell the coach so they can decide who does what.

### Question 62

Coming a little early lets you set out your books so you're ready the moment class starts.

### Question 63

Before you say yes to helping, you check you're really free, and if you promise, you show up.

### Question 64

If you're too sick for school, you call the office in the morning so they know, instead of just not showing up.

### Question 65

When you call in sick, you say what's wrong and when you might be back, so people can plan.

### Question 66

Tell someone you'll be absent before the day starts, like telling your coach before the game, not after.

### Question 67

If the goalie knows early they can't play, the team can find a backup before the game, not after it starts.

### Question 68

If you can't come because you're needed at home, you call the person in charge early so they can find help.

### Question 69

You tell the person in charge, like telling the teacher, not just any classmate.

### Question 70

If you're a little late, you tell someone, then get to work and help out however they need.

### Question 71

If you're the one with the key but you're too sick, you call for help right away instead of spreading germs or leaving everyone locked out.

### Question 72

What people think of you comes from many things together, like how you look, how you act, and how you talk.

### Question 73

Saying hello clearly with a smile and telling someone your name makes them feel welcome.

### Question 74

You feel safer telling a secret to someone who looks and acts trustworthy. Patients feel the same way about their health details.

### Question 75

You iron your shirt and wipe off your name tag for the next day so you look neat again.
